Knowledge Base & Insights

Understanding inflation

Inflation is the gradual decline of purchasing power of a given currency over time. A quantitative estimate of the rate at which the decline in purchasing power occurs can be reflected in the increase of an average price level of a basket of selected goods and services in an economy over some period of time. Our Inflation Calculator helps you visualize exactly how this economic phenomenon impacts your hard-earned money.

How Inflation Affects Purchasing Power

This tool uses standard compound interest formulas in reverse to calculate the future value and the erosion of purchasing power. There are two primary perspectives when dealing with inflation:

Future Cost: This answers the question: "If an item costs $10,000 today, how much will the exact same item cost in 10 years?" If inflation averages 3.5% per year, you will need more dollars to buy that same item.

Purchasing Power: This answers the question: "If I hide $10,000 under my mattress today, what will it be worth in 10 years?" Because prices rise, your static $10,000 buys fewer goods and services in the future.

The Inflation Formula

To calculate the Future Cost of an item currently priced at P, with an annual inflation rate of r over t years, we use a simple compounding formula.

Similarly, to calculate the future Purchasing Power of an amount P held today, we use the inverse formula.

Real World Example

Let's look at a realistic scenario where you are considering keeping your money in cash versus investing it. Imagine you place $50,000 in a safe in your home, intending to use it for a down payment on a house in 15 years.

Purchasing Power Loss Calculation
Example Parameters:
  • Current Amount: $50,000
  • Annual Inflation Rate: 4%
  • Time Period: 15 Years
Sequential Steps:
  1. Convert the annual inflation rate to a decimal: r = 0.04.
  2. Calculate the denominator: (1 + 0.04)^15 ≈ 1.8009.
  3. Apply the formula: Purchasing Power = $50,000 / 1.8009.
Takeaway Result:The purchasing power of your $50,000 drops to just $27,763. You have essentially lost $22,237 of value simply by not investing the money to pace with or beat inflation.

Formula Used

Future Cost = P × (1 + r)^n
Purchasing Power = P / (1 + r)^n

Variables

P
Current amount
r
Annual inflation rate
n
Time period in years

Example Calculation

  1. 1Suppose an item costs $10,000 today. If inflation averages 3.5% per year for 10 years:
  2. 2Future Cost = $10,000 × (1 + 0.035)^10 = $14,105.99
  3. 3This means you will need $14,106 in 10 years to buy what $10,000 buys today.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is inflation?

Inflation is the rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services is rising, and, subsequently, purchasing power is falling. Central banks attempt to limit inflation, and avoid deflation, in order to keep the economy running smoothly.

How does inflation affect my savings?

Inflation decreases the purchasing power of money over time. If your savings account earns a 1% interest rate but inflation is at 3%, the real value of your savings is decreasing by roughly 2% per year.

What is the difference between Future Cost and Purchasing Power?

Future Cost tells you how much money you will need in the future to buy something that costs a certain amount today. Purchasing Power tells you how much a specific amount of money today will be worth in the future, measured in today's goods.

What is considered a 'normal' inflation rate?

Historically, central banks like the U.S. Federal Reserve have targeted an inflation rate of about 2% per year. This is considered a healthy rate for economic growth without eroding purchasing power too quickly.

How can I protect my money from inflation?

Investing in assets that traditionally outpace inflation, such as stocks, real estate, or Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), can help preserve and grow your purchasing power over time.

Does inflation affect all goods equally?

No, inflation rates can vary widely between different sectors. For example, healthcare and education costs have historically risen much faster than the general inflation rate, while the cost of electronics has often decreased.

What causes inflation?

Inflation can be caused by demand-pull (when demand exceeds supply), cost-push (when production costs increase), and built-in inflation (wage-price spirals). Increases in the money supply can also drive inflation.

Can inflation be negative?

Yes, negative inflation is called deflation. While it sounds good for consumers initially because prices drop, prolonged deflation can lead to severe economic problems, such as reduced spending, lower wages, and higher unemployment.
